rubric.name: CC Audience Awareness
rubric.description: Every CC'd person is there for a reason, and the email is crafted knowing they will read it. The primary recipient gets the ask; the CC'd audience gets a deliberate signal — accountability, visibility, or alignment.

dimensions.label: Each CC'd person receives a specific signal from the email (accountability, awareness, endorsement)
Nothing in the email reveals information inappropriate for any CC'd reader
The primary recipient and their specific ask are unambiguous despite the CC'd audience
The CC list itself sends a message — the choice of who is included is deliberate

negative_examples: Scoring a CFO CC lower because the email doesn't directly address the CFO, when the CFO's silent presence is itself the intended signal
Treating an explicit sub-instruction to a CC'd person as inherently superior to a deliberate ambient signal — both can be correct depending on what the email needs to accomplish
Requiring that CC'd audiences receive active tasks or named acknowledgments to score highly on this criterion
rubric.clarification: CC Audience Awareness is about whether the CC list and email content are crafted with full awareness of every reader. A CFO CC'd silently can be just as intentional and powerful as one who receives a direct instruction — the question is whether the drafter knew what signal the CFO would receive and chose it deliberately. The grader should evaluate intentionality and appropriateness of the signal, not whether the signal was explicit versus ambient.

rubric.name: Directive Clarity
rubric.description: Non-negotiable requests use direct language, never conditional framing. 'Please submit by Friday' not 'Would you be able to submit by Friday?' Conditional language is reserved exclusively for genuinely optional items.

dimensions.label: Required actions do not use 'if possible', 'would you be able to', or 'it would be great if'
Truly optional items use optionality language to distinguish them from requirements
The level of directness matches the sender's authority relative to the recipient

negative_examples: Flagging 'I'd ask that you' as a potential false conditional when the sender and recipient are organizational peers
Treating all softened language as conditional framing — softening for peer register is different from hedging a directive to a subordinate
Applying the same directness standard to lateral communications as to downward communications
rubric.clarification: The no-false-conditionals rule applies to directives issued downward in the hierarchy. When a COO addresses a CFO, the appropriate register is different — 'I'd ask that you hold the package' is a directive, not a suggestion, and the CFO will read it that way. The criterion is about not undermining authority through hedging, not about eliminating all register-appropriate softening in peer or upward communications. Authority-matches-ask means calibrating directness to the actual power relationship, which the Round 2 draft did correctly.

rubric.name: Recipient-Interest Framing
rubric.description: Requests are positioned as serving the recipient's interest, even when the ask primarily benefits the sender. The reframe must be genuine — not a transparent manipulation.

dimensions.label: The email explains how the ask serves the recipient or their team, not just the sender

Avoids 'we need this for our planning' when 'this helps your team plan' is more accurate

rubric.name: Voice Matching

rubric_snapshot.user_goals_summary: Writes emails that navigate organizational power dynamics with precision. Every word is chosen for how it lands with the primary recipient AND the CC'd audience. Treats email as a tool of organizational choreography, not just communication.

rubric.name: CC Audience Awareness
rubric.description: Every CC'd person is there for a reason, and the email is crafted knowing they will read it. The primary recipient gets the ask; the CC'd audience gets a deliberate signal — accountability, visibility, or alignment.

dimensions.label: Each CC'd person receives a specific signal from the email (accountability, awareness, endorsement)
Nothing in the email reveals information inappropriate for any CC'd reader
The primary recipient and their specific ask are unambiguous despite the CC'd audience
The CC list itself sends a message — the choice of who is included is deliberate

negative_examples: Scoring a CFO CC lower because the email doesn't directly address the CFO, when the CFO's silent presence is itself the intended signal
Treating an explicit sub-instruction to a CC'd person as inherently superior to a deliberate ambient signal — both can be correct depending on what the email needs to accomplish
Requiring that CC'd audiences receive active tasks or named acknowledgments to score highly on this criterion
rubric.clarification: CC Audience Awareness is about whether the CC list and email content are crafted with full awareness of every reader. A CFO CC'd silently can be just as intentional and powerful as one who receives a direct instruction — the question is whether the drafter knew what signal the CFO would receive and chose it deliberately. The grader should evaluate intentionality and appropriateness of the signal, not whether the signal was explicit versus ambient.

rubric.name: Directive Clarity
rubric.description: Non-negotiable requests use direct language, never conditional framing. 'Please submit by Friday' not 'Would you be able to submit by Friday?' Conditional language is reserved exclusively for genuinely optional items.

dimensions.label: Required actions do not use 'if possible', 'would you be able to', or 'it would be great if'
Truly optional items use optionality language to distinguish them from requirements
The level of directness matches the sender's authority relative to the recipient

negative_examples: Flagging 'I'd ask that you' as a potential false conditional when the sender and recipient are organizational peers
Treating all softened language as conditional framing — softening for peer register is different from hedging a directive to a subordinate
Applying the same directness standard to lateral communications as to downward communications
rubric.clarification: The no-false-conditionals rule applies to directives issued downward in the hierarchy. When a COO addresses a CFO, the appropriate register is different — 'I'd ask that you hold the package' is a directive, not a suggestion, and the CFO will read it that way. The criterion is about not undermining authority through hedging, not about eliminating all register-appropriate softening in peer or upward communications. Authority-matches-ask means calibrating directness to the actual power relationship, which the Round 2 draft did correctly.

rubric.name: Recipient-Interest Framing
rubric.description: Requests are positioned as serving the recipient's interest, even when the ask primarily benefits the sender. The reframe must be genuine — not a transparent manipulation.

dimensions.label: The email explains how the ask serves the recipient or their team, not just the sender

rubric.name: Voice Matching
rubric.description: When writing on behalf of an executive, the email sounds like that person — mirroring their vocabulary, sentence length, and communication style — not like a generic professional email.

dimensions.label: Uses words and phrases the named executive would actually use

negative_examples: Giving a draft a 5 or 6 because the COO's name is a placeholder, even when the draft has a clearly distinct, non-generic voice
